where: Section 2, sentence after the flange formula
problem: The sentence "Hydraulic losses make Hm e." is truncated and meaningless. The key inequality Hm < He — the whole point of the section — is lost.
fix: Hydraulic losses make Hm less than He, so Hm < He and ηman < 1.

problem: The answer says leakage and mechanical losses consume part of the impeller work and so lower Hm. Mechanical losses occur outside the fluid (bearings, gland, shaft) and do not reduce the head imparted per unit weight; leakage lowers the delivered discharge (a volumetric effect), not the head per unit weight. Only hydraulic losses inside impeller and casing (friction, shock, eddy formation) make Hm smaller than He.
fix: Hm < He because of hydraulic losses inside the impeller and casing — vane and casing friction, shock at entry and exit, and eddy formation. Leakage lowers the useful discharge (volumetric efficiency), and mechanical losses lower the shaft power utilisation; neither reduces the head per unit weight. The lead sentence "The rest is lost to friction, shock and leakage" should be reworded the same way.

problem: Calling manometric efficiency simply "(hydraulic) efficiency" is loose. Many books reserve hydraulic efficiency for the impeller alone, i.e. the ratio of actual head to the ideal Euler head after allowing for slip, which is a different number.
fix: Say: ηman = Hm/He is the manometric efficiency; some syllabi call this the hydraulic efficiency of the pump, while others use hydraulic efficiency for the impeller-only ratio.
